title: JAMA Study: ICE Detention Death Rate Reached 22-Year High in Early FY2026
excerpt: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of the American Medical Association found the ICE detainee mortality rate hit a 22-year high in the opening months of fiscal year 2026, reaching 88.9 deaths per 100,000 person-years. Researchers attributed the spike to systemic weaknesses in medical care compounded by Trump administration policy changes.
content:
A research letter published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) on April 17, 2026, analyzed mortality rates among ICE detainees from fiscal year 2004 through January 19, 2026. The study found 272 total deaths over that 22-year period.

The mortality rate for partial FY2026 reached 88.9 per 100,000 person-years—the highest recorded in the 22-year study period, exceeding even the COVID-19 pandemic spike. The rate is nearly seven times the FY2023 level of 13.0 per 100,000.

  • Annual death rates had declined from a peak of 127.7 in FY2004 to a low of 13.0 in FY2023, before climbing steeply to 47.5 in FY2025 and 88.9 in partial FY2026.
  • Between FY2021 and early 2026, cardiovascular causes accounted for 18.5% of deaths; suicide for 10.8%.
  • Authors wrote the findings "suggest not isolated lapses but systemic weaknesses in medical care, mental health protection, and mortality review in a population wholly dependent on the state."
  • Researchers cited disrupted oversight mechanisms, rapid detention expansion with overcrowding, and potentially delayed medical care as contributing factors.
The causes of death in individual cases "are identifiable and amenable to intervention" and "are things that any doctor in the community routinely prevents deaths from," said co-author Sanjay Basu, MD, PhD.
